\chapter{The Ten Persian Digits}
\label{ch:fa-digits}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read and write the ten Persian digits, read a price, a page number and a telephone number off an Iranian page, and say which way a number runs inside a right-to-left line.}

Ten signs across four lessons, grouped by what makes each pair hard: the reversed direction, the one-tooth pair, the three Arabic draws differently, and the mirror pair.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sefr yek]{\fa{۰} \fa{۱} — two digits, and a direction that reverses}

\label{lesson:FA-W19-digits-zero-one}



\begin{quote}
Which way does a Persian line run? Say \textbf{yek}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes, and the direction}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{۰}} — \emph{sefr}, zero  \textbf{\fa{۱}} — \emph{yek}, one
\end{quote}

Persian has its own ten digit signs, and every price ticket, telephone number and page number in Iran is written in them. A reader who can say \textbf{yek} and cannot read \textbf{\fa{۱}} still cannot read a price.

\textbf{\fa{۰}} is a \textbf{dot}, not a ring. Fix that first, because a European eye reads a dot as a decimal point — and Persian's nine is the ring.

Now the part no earlier chapter has had to say: \textbf{numbers run left to right, inside a line that runs right to left.} Ten is \textbf{\fa{۱۰}} — one, then zero, in the European order — while the words around it move the other way. The page changes direction at the number and changes back after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\fa{۰}} — a dot; \textbf{\fa{۱}} — a stroke
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{۱۰}} — \emph{dah}, ten, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do se]{\fa{۲} \fa{۳} — one tooth apart}

\label{lesson:FA-W19-digits-two-three}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\fa{۰}} and \textbf{\fa{۱}}, then read \textbf{\fa{۱۰}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{۲}} — \emph{do}, two  \textbf{\fa{۳}} — \emph{se}, three
\end{quote}

\textbf{\fa{۳}} is \textbf{\fa{۲}} with one more tooth. That is the whole difference, and it is small enough that the two have to be written as a pair rather than one at a time — say \emph{do} and \emph{se} aloud as the hand makes them and the shapes stop competing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\fa{۲}}, then \textbf{\fa{۳}} beside it
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{۱۲}}, \textbf{\fa{۱۳}}, \textbf{\fa{۲۳}}, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chahâr panj shesh]{\fa{۴} \fa{۵} \fa{۶} — the three Persian keeps for itself}

\label{lesson:FA-W19-digits-four-five-six}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\fa{۲}} and \textbf{\fa{۳}}, and say which has the extra tooth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{۴}} — \emph{chahâr}, four  \textbf{\fa{۵}} — \emph{panj}, five  \textbf{\fa{۶}} — \emph{shesh}, six
\end{quote}

These three are the reason this chapter exists as more than a list.

Seven of the ten digits are drawn the same way in Persian and in Arabic. \textbf{\fa{۴}}, \textbf{\fa{۵}} and \textbf{\fa{۶}} are not: Arabic writes those three with quite different shapes. A reader who picked up the digits from an Arabic book will read an Iranian price wrongly at exactly these three places and nowhere else.

If you drill three of the ten harder than the rest, drill these.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\fa{۴}}, \textbf{\fa{۵}}, \textbf{\fa{۶}}, saying \emph{chahâr}, \emph{panj}, \emph{shesh}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{۱۴}}, \textbf{\fa{۱۵}}, \textbf{\fa{۱۶}}, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[haft hasht noh]{\fa{۷} \fa{۸} \fa{۹} — a mirror pair, and the ring}

\label{lesson:FA-W19-digits-seven-eight-nine}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\fa{۴}}, \textbf{\fa{۵}}, \textbf{\fa{۶}} — the three Arabic draws differently.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{۷}} — \emph{haft}, seven  \textbf{\fa{۸}} — \emph{hasht}, eight  \textbf{\fa{۹}} — \emph{noh}, nine
\end{quote}

\textbf{\fa{۷}} and \textbf{\fa{۸}} are mirror images of each other, one opening upward and one downward. Write them as a pair, every time, and the mirror stops being a problem — the same trick that worked on \textbf{\fa{۲}} and \textbf{\fa{۳}}.

\textbf{\fa{۹}} is a \textbf{ring} with a tail, and this is where a dot-shaped zero pays off. Had \textbf{\fa{۰}} been a ring too, the page would carry two rings and no way to separate them.

Ten signs, four lessons. The set is closed.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\fa{۷}} and \textbf{\fa{۸}} as a pair, then \textbf{\fa{۹}}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\fa{۰} \fa{۱} \fa{۲} \fa{۳} \fa{۴} \fa{۵} \fa{۶} \fa{۷} \fa{۸} \fa{۹}} once, slowly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/persian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Persian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — reading the figures}

\label{lesson:FA-C19-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to twenty, then say which way digits run inside a Persian line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Read all ten signs shuffled and say each as a Persian word.
  \item Read \textbf{\fa{۱۰}}, \textbf{\fa{۱۱}}, \textbf{\fa{۲۰}} and \textbf{\fa{۱۰۰}} and say each — \emph{dah}, \emph{yâzdah}, \emph{bist}, \emph{sad}.
  \item Hear ten amounts named and write each in Persian figures.
  \item Write the ten signs from dictation, out of order, and check \textbf{\fa{۴}}, \textbf{\fa{۵}} and \textbf{\fa{۶}} against the models rather than against memory.
\end{enumerate}

Say what a reader can now do that could not be done four chapters ago: read a price, a page number and a telephone number off an Iranian page.
